planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring so roots establish well before the first winter cold snap.

directions: This exceptionally cold-tolerant palmetto selection was discovered growing outdoors in Birmingham, Alabama, well outside the normal range for trunking sabals, and has since been prized by cold-climate palm growers for surviving hard freezes that damage typical Sabal minor. It develops a short, thick, often mostly subterranean trunk topped by a dense crown of stiff, deeply costapalmate blue-green fronds. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and water regularly the first two seasons to establish a deep root system, after which it tolerates both drought and occasional standing water. Because it grows very slowly and resents root disturbance, choose its permanent site carefully and avoid transplanting mature specimens.

planting.note: Plant in spring from containers and mulch the crown the first winter until the root system matures.

directions: Collected from a wild population in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, this is the most cold-hardy form of dwarf palmetto in cultivation, tolerating brief drops well below 0°F once established, which makes it a favorite for pushing hardy-palm plantings into colder zones than typical Gulf Coast sabals. It stays essentially trunkless, sending up a dense clump of fan-shaped, silvery-green to blue-green leaves directly from an underground rhizome, and slowly suckers to form a wide colony over many years. Grow in part shade to full sun in average to wet soil; it is naturally an understory and bottomland plant, so it tolerates heavier, poorly drained sites better than most cold-hardy palms. Established clumps need little care beyond removing old fronds and are essentially pest-free.

planting.note: Transplant young palms in spring so they have a full growing season to establish before facing winter cold.

directions: Propagated from a naturalized, long-established population of windmill palms growing along Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, this strain is selected for enhanced cold hardiness beyond typical nursery-grown Trachycarpus fortunei, having survived winter lows that damage or kill ordinary stock. It forms a single fibrous, burlap-wrapped trunk topped with a crown of large, dark green, fan-shaped fronds, growing slowly into a striking small tree. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, fertile soil and water deeply during the first two years to speed establishment and trunk formation. Once established it needs only routine removal of spent fronds and occasional feeding to remain a low-maintenance, long-lived landscape specimen.
